title: Minimal and secure runtime images
description: Choose the right base image for production, understand the Alpine versus Debian trade-offs, and harden runtime images to reduce attack surface.

data.text: The base image you choose becomes the foundation of every security control, every performance optimization, and every compatibility test downstream. A large base image like `ubuntu:latest` carries thousands of packages you do not need, while a minimal image like `alpine` or `distroless` reduces both attack surface and image size.

Base images fall along a spectrum from full operating systems to almost nothing. Understanding where each option sits helps you make informed trade-offs between compatibility, tooling, size, and security.

cards.title: Full distro images
cards.description: Complete operating system images such as `ubuntu:22.04` or `debian:12`.
pros: Easy to debug inside the container

cards.title: Slim distro images
cards.description: Stripped-down variants such as `debian:12-slim` that remove docs and some utilities.
cons: glibc-based musl differences do not apply

cards.title: Alpine images
cards.description: Tiny images based on Alpine Linux and musl libc, such as `node:20-alpine`.
cons: Some native binaries may not work

cards.title: Distroless images
cards.description: Google's distroless images contain only the application and its runtime dependencies, no shell or package manager.

cards.title: Scratch images
cards.description: The empty base image. Only truly static binaries can run on `scratch`.

data.text: Every package in an image is a potential vulnerability. The more packages you include, the more Common Vulnerabilities and Exposures (CVEs) apply to your image. A minimal image dramatically reduces the number of packages that need scanning, patching, and monitoring.

data.title: Image scanners expose the difference
data.text: Tools like Trivy and Grype routinely report hundreds of CVEs in `ubuntu:latest` and much fewer in `alpine` or distroless images. Fewer packages mean fewer vulnerabilities to track, patch, and explain to auditors.

Always pin base images to a specific digest or a specific minor version. Floating tags such as `latest` or `20` change over time and can silently introduce new packages, new vulnerabilities, or behavioral differences into your build.

data.title: Pinned base image with digest
data.content: Pin both the tag and the digest for maximum reproducibility. The digest is a SHA256 hash of the image manifest.

data.text: Digests are long and awkward to type, so many teams use version-pinned tags in Dockerfiles and enforce digest verification in CI. Both approaches are valid. The important thing is to avoid floating tags in production.

Alpine Linux uses musl libc instead of glibc. Most interpreted languages such as Python, Node.js, and Go work fine on Alpine, but native extensions and dynamically linked binaries may fail. Test thoroughly before choosing Alpine for C++, .NET native, or other native-dependent workloads.

After choosing a base image, harden it by removing unnecessary packages, disabling root execution where possible, and cleaning up package manager caches. Each of these steps reduces both the attack surface and the image size.

data.title: Runtime hardening checklist
items: Remove the `curl`, `wget`, and `git` packages after dependencies are installed
Clear package manager caches in the same RUN instruction that installs packages
Create a non-root user and set it as the container's default user
Set `USER` before the final CMD so the process runs without root privileges
Remove the `ENTRYPOINT` or `CMD` shell forms to avoid implicit shell execution

data.title: Hardened runtime stage
data.content: A hardened Dockerfile creates a non-root user, removes package caches, and avoids running the application as root.
data.code:
FROM node:20-alpine

WORKDIR /app
COPY package.json package-lock.json ./
RUN npm ci --production \
    && addgroup -g 1001 -S appgroup \
    && adduser -u 1001 -S appuser -G appgroup \
    && chown -R appuser:appgroup /app

USER appuser
COPY . .
EXPOSE 3000
CMD ["node", "server.js"]

data.text: Distroless and scratch for maximum security

Distroless images contain only the application binary and its dynamic library dependencies. There is no shell, no package manager, and no SSH server. An attacker who gains code execution inside a distroless container has very few tools available for lateral movement.

data.title: Debugging distroless containers
data.text: Because distroless images lack a shell, you cannot `docker exec` into them for debugging. Use `kubectl debug` with an ephemeral debug container, or temporarily switch to a debug image in non-production environments.

data.title: Key takeaways
points: Base image choice affects size, compatibility, and security
Pin base images to digests or specific minor versions to prevent silent drift
Alpine is small and secure but may not support native binaries that depend on glibc
Distroless images offer maximum security by removing the shell and package manager
Always create a non-root user and run the application without root privileges
data.takeaway: The smallest compatible base image is usually the most secure, but compatibility must be verified before adopting Alpine or distroless in production.
